sections.body_md:
A linear program asks for the best value of a linear function on a set cut out by linear equalities and inequalities. Standard form is one shape of that question: minimize \(c^T x\), keep every constraint an equality \(Ax = b\), and require \(x \ge 0\). The shape is a rewriting, not a smaller class of problems.

A maximization becomes a minimization when the cost is replaced by its negative. The two programs share their feasible points, and the optimal values are negatives of each other. An upper bound \(a^T x \le \beta\) becomes an equality by adding a slack that records the unused room. A lower bound \(a^T x \ge \beta\) becomes an equality by subtracting a surplus. A variable that may be negative is the difference of two nonnegative variables. An absolute value in a constraint splits into two ordinary linear inequalities.

After those rewrites the feasible set is the original one, described so that a square block of columns can be a basis. The names of the new variables are bookkeeping. What matters is which equalities they create and which signs they are required to keep.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Standard form is
\[
\text{minimize } c^T x \quad \text{subject to } Ax = b,\ x \ge 0.
\]
An upper bound and a lower bound become
\[
a^T x + s = \beta, \qquad a^T x - s = \beta,
\]
with \(s \ge 0\). A free variable splits as \(x = x^+ - x^-\) with both parts nonnegative. Then \(\lvert x \rvert = x^+ + x^-\) once a basic solution is chosen so that at least one of the two parts is zero, which a nondegenerate basis does on its own.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take the upper bound \(8x + y \le 41\), and evaluate it at \((x, y) = (2, 6)\). The left-hand side is \(16 + 6 = 22\). The slack is the gap from 22 up to 41.

The ribbon slack is 19. The equality form is \(8x + y + s = 41\) with \(s \ge 0\). At this point \(s = 19\). Moving the same point onto a different right-hand side would change the slack and would not change the rule that defines it. A surplus would have been the wrong extra variable, because the inequality bounds the linear form from above.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The usual sign error is to add a slack on a lower bound, or to subtract one on an upper bound. The extra variable has to restore equality in the direction the inequality allows. A second error is to keep a maximization and call the form standard. The geometry is the same only after the cost changes sign. A third is to split a free variable and then require the two pieces to sum to zero. That forces both pieces to zero and deletes the variable. Both pieces are nonnegative, and their difference is free. Putting a slack and a surplus on the same inequality adds a needless degree of freedom.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A planar picture of the same program reads the optimum off a polygon, including the cases where the best value is attained on a whole edge, where the set is empty, and where the objective runs off to infinity. In any dimension the feasible set is a polyhedron, and the candidates that matter are its extreme points. Those extreme points are exactly the basic feasible solutions of the standard form written here. The dual linear program is built from this same equality form.
